def cheapest_item_name(names, values):
    """Every morning the stallkeeper of the old covered market chalks a
    fresh price board: one column of item names, one column of asking
    prices. Step up, read the board, and call out the day's bargain so
    the barkers can shout it across the square. names is a list of
    strings and values is a list of ints of the same length; names[i]
    and values[i] describe the same item.

    Treat each value as the price the keeper wants for that item, in
    coppers. Do not be startled by odd numbers on the board: a zero
    means a giveaway promotion, and a negative figure means the keeper
    will pay you to cart the thing off — from where you stand, both are
    simply very low prices. Return the name of the item with the
    SMALLEST value; if several items tie for the smallest value return
    the one appearing first; return None for empty lists.

    That covers the slow days as well: when the market is shuttered and
    the board hangs blank, there is simply no bargain to cry. The
    barkers trust your call completely, so the examples below show
    exactly the sort of boards you will face — a lone item on a
    giveaway, a mixed board where the keeper pays you to take the ax,
    and the empty board of a closed market.

    >>> cheapest_item_name(['refill'], [0])
    'refill'
    >>> cheapest_item_name(['ax', 'bolt', 'eel'], [-2, 0, 38])
    'ax'
    >>> cheapest_item_name([], [])
    """
